blogs.title: The Commissioner's Exclusive Domain: Parsing Private Rights to Penalties Under the MPWA
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's statutory interpretation of the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA). It focuses on the court's distinction between an employee's right to recover unpaid wages versus the Commissioner's exclusive authority to assess 'average daily wage penalties.' The analysis will explore how the court utilized the 'knows how' canon of construction—comparing § 181.101 to other Minnesota statutes where the legislature explicitly granted private penalty rights—to conclude that private plaintiffs cannot bypass the Commissioner to seek these specific punitive damages.

blogs.title: Voluntary Cessation vs. Mootness: The Jurisdictional Trap in Wage-and-Class Actions
blogs.description: Focusing on the MFLSA claim, this entry examines the complex interplay between Article III standing, mootness, and the 'voluntary cessation' doctrine. While Cohen received full compensation for back wages and liquidated damages, the court vacated summary judgment to determine if his claim for civil penalties (payable to the state, not him) survives. The post will dissect why payment of individual damages does not automatically moot a claim for statutory penalties intended to deter future conduct, and what factual findings regarding Consilio's current policies are now required on remand to establish a live controversy.

blogs.title: Procedural Pitfalls: Waiver, Amendment, and the Limits of Summary Judgment Briefing
blogs.description: This post critiques the procedural missteps that led to the dismissal of Cohen's MWTA notice claim and his request for injunctive relief. It highlights two critical lessons for practitioners: first, the danger of failing to develop legal arguments with citations in summary judgment responses, leading to waiver; and second, the impermissibility of introducing new claims or altering the scope of requested injunctive relief (such as changing from specific policy modifications to a blanket rescission) for the first time in an opposition brief rather than through a formal amendment under Rule 15(a).
